# Results — Study 113 (Gold-Silver-Ratio) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The gold/silver ratio
(GLD/SLV ETF price ratio) z-score mean-reversion strategy: enter long-spread when the
rolling 252-day z-score exceeds ±1.5 (ratio at a 16-month extreme), exit when z reverts
within ±0.5. No short-selling of futures — ETF-only (long GLD/short SLV or vice versa).
Compared against a random-direction control on identical entry/exit dates. As-of
**2026-06-13**. GLD and SLV daily data from 2010-01-04 to 2026-06-12 via Yahoo Finance.*

## Data stamp

| Ticker | Window | n bars | Fingerprint |
|---|---|--:|---|
| GLD (SPDR Gold Shares) | 2010-01-04 → 2026-06-12 | 4,136 | `fb68a1c04a2b` |
| SLV (iShares Silver Trust) | 2010-01-04 → 2026-06-12 | 4,136 | `1dbb4be8cc36` |

GLD/SLV ratio range: **3.17 – 12.55**, mean **7.36** over the full period. (The GLD/SLV
ratio ≈ spot gold/silver ratio / 10, because GLD holds 1/10 oz gold and SLV ≈ 1 oz silver;
the ETF ratio is proportional to the spot ratio and inherits the same mean-reversion structure.)

## Structural tests — is there a mean-reverting ratio to exploit?

These three tests are the *prerequisite* for the folk trade. All three fail:

| Test | Statistic | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| ADF on GLD/SLV ratio | p = 0.2158 | **Fails to reject unit root** — ratio looks like a random walk |
| OU half-life (AR fit) | **301 trading days** (~15 months) | Extremely slow reversion even if any |
| Engle-Granger cointegration | p = 0.7362 | **Not cointegrated** — two trending series, not a mean-reverting pair |

> The ratio is not statistically stationary (ADF p = 0.22), gold and silver are not
> cointegrated over 2010–2026 (p = 0.74), and even under the AR(1) model the implied
> half-life is 301 trading days — so any position taken today might wait 15 months
> for a "reversion" that may never come.

## Strategy results — primary: enter |z₂₅₂| > 1.5, exit |z| < 0.5

With 16 years of data and a 252-day z-score, only **26 round-trip trades** are generated.
The average holding period is **78 trading days** (~4 months). This alone signals extreme
trading aridity — fewer than 2 signals per year.

| Arm | n | win-rate | mean (bps/trade) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Z-score reversion strategy** | 26 | **65.4%** | **+144.2** | **+1.77** |
| Random direction (control) | 26 | 53.8% | +18.9 | +0.21 |

- The HAC t-stat is **+1.77** — below the desk's |t| ≥ 2 inference bar. With only 26
  trades, the standard error is enormous and the estimate is fragile.
- Point estimate is positive (+144 bps per trade gross), suggesting some reversion effect,
  but it is **not statistically robust** by the desk's standard.
- The strategy does beat the random control by +125 bps (point estimate), but the
  absolute trade count (26 in 16 years) limits inference severely.

### Sensitivity: tighter threshold (enter |z| > 2.0)

| Arm | n | win-rate | mean (bps/trade) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Z-score reversion (|z|>2) | 19 | 73.7% | +240.1 | +2.74 |

With only **19 trades** the t-stat of 2.74 appears to clear the bar, but with n=19 the
Newey-West estimator has very limited degrees of freedom and is unreliable. A single bad
trade can swing the t-stat by more than 1 unit. This is an overfitted look-alike of a
signal, not a robust edge.

## Cost analysis

The strategy trades infrequently (~1.6 times/year) with ~78-day holds. Transaction costs
are small in relative terms but the gross edge itself is uncertain:

| round-trip cost | net mean (bps/trade) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0.0 bps (gross) | +144.2 | +1.77 |
| 5.0 bps | +139.2 | +1.71 |
| 10.0 bps | +134.2 | +1.65 |
| 20.0 bps | +124.2 | +1.53 |

Costs are not the killer here (only 2 trades/yr, long holds) — the tiny sample size and
failure of the stationarity tests are.

## Buy-and-hold benchmark

Over 2010–2026, both metals delivered comparable returns:

| Asset | Total log-return | Annualised |
|---|--:|--:|
| GLD (gold ETF) | +125.9% | +8.0%/yr |
| SLV (silver ETF) | +126.9% | +8.0%/yr |

The metals are both good long-term stores of value. The spread strategy adds complexity
and requires active management for comparable (but uncertain) total returns.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery works when reversion is real

On a deterministic synthetic pair with a planted OU mean-reversion speed, the same
z-score strategy recovers an edge over the random-direction control — the machine is
a faithful mean-reversion harvester. The real tape simply lacks statistical evidence of
the required reversion structure.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** HAC *t* = +1.77 on 26 trades over 16 years, below the |t| ≥ 2
  inference bar. The structural tests (ADF p = 0.22, Engle-Granger p = 0.74, half-life
  = 301 days) do not support the folk trade's premise that the ratio mean-reverts
  reliably. Point estimate is positive but statistically inconclusive.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** ~1.6 trades/year with ~78-day average holds. Costs are
  not the problem, but the extreme aridity of signals and the non-stationarity of the
  ratio make this a slow, unreliable rotation that underperforms a simple buy-and-hold
  of either metal during the waiting periods.
- **Is the ratio actually mean-reverting? — NOT SUPPORTED.** The ADF test fails to
  reject a unit root, the pair is not cointegrated, and the implied half-life of 301
  days is so slow as to be practically indistinguishable from a random walk at any
  trading horizon.
